The exact cause of leukemia is not well understood, but it is believed to involve a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Conversely, acute myeloid leukemia (AML) affects adults more frequently and involves the rapid growth of abnormal myeloid cells. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), typically a disease of the elderly, progresses slowly and affects lymphocyte cells. Lastly, chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is marked by the uncontrolled growth of myeloid cells in the bone marrow and, gradually, in the blood. Understanding these variations is essential for customizing patient care and optimizing outcomes in leukemia treatment.

Targeted therapy exploits vulnerabilities in cancer cells, for instance, specific proteins or genes, to interrupt their ability to grow. Bone marrow transplant is typically considered when other treatments haven’t been successful. It involves replacing the diseased bone marrow with healthy marrow from a donor, potentially leading to a cure. Each treatment carries its own set of risks and benefits, and the healthcare team works closely with the patient to determine the most appropriate approach.
